sections.content: You've already met the past participle used as an adjective — Core Unit 2 introduced forms like *elkészített étel* ("the prepared food"), where a single word replaces a whole relative clause ("the food that was prepared"). This Citizenship unit reuses exactly that pattern, but for a different purpose: giving historical figures and events fixed epithets, the kind Hungarian uses constantly — *a megkeresztelt fejedelem* ("the baptized prince"), *a megkoronázott király* ("the crowned king"). You'll meet this pattern again and again while talking about István, so it's worth being fully comfortable with it before going further.

sections.title: Verb -> participle (used as an adjective)
rows: to raise, bring up -> raised, brought up

items.spanish: A megkeresztelt Vajk később az István nevet kapta.
items.english: The baptized Vajk later received the name István.

items.spanish: Géza fejedelem az elfogadott keresztény hitet fia házassága által is igyekezett megerősíteni.
items.english: Prince Géza tried to strengthen the newly accepted Christian faith also through his son's marriage.

items.spanish: A megkeresztelt fejedelem szoros kapcsolatot keresett a keresztény Nyugattal.
items.english: The baptized prince sought a close relationship with the Christian West.

sections.content: Unlike English past participles used as adjectives ("the baptized prince"), Hungarian's is invariant: it never changes for the noun's number or case — only the noun itself inflects. *a megkeresztelt fejedelem* ("the baptized prince") becomes *a megkeresztelt fejedelmek* ("the baptized princes") — the participle *megkeresztelt* stays exactly the same.
